title: The Light of the World and Before Abraham, I Am
summary: The chapter opens with the account of a woman caught in adultery, whom Jesus refuses to condemn while telling her to sin no more; this passage is missing from the earliest manuscripts of John. In the temple courts Jesus then declares, “I am the light of the world,” and argues with his opponents about his testimony, his origin, and true freedom. The debate grows fierce over who is a true child of Abraham, and it ends when Jesus says, “before Abraham was born, I am,” and the crowd picks up stones.
story:
We are still in Jerusalem during or just after the Feast of Tabernacles, and the arguments of chapter 7 intensify. Chapter 7 asked where Jesus comes from; chapter 8 answers with the boldest claims yet. He is the light of the world, he comes from above, he speaks what the Father taught him, and he existed before Abraham. In the earliest manuscripts 8:12 follows directly on 7:52, so that Jesus' claim to be the light answers the leaders' sneer that no prophet comes from Galilee.

The chapter records a sharp breakdown. It begins with many believing in him (8:30-31) and ends with those same hearers trying to stone him, which shows how shallow belief can turn to hostility when Jesus names what discipleship will cost. The dispute over fatherhood, whether the hearers are children of Abraham, of God, or of the devil, is among the most painful texts in the New Testament and needs careful reading. The chapter also prepares for what follows. The light of the world will give sight to a man born blind in chapter 9, and the stones taken up in 8:59 will be taken up again in 10:31. The story of the woman caught in adultery, placed at the head of the chapter by later copyists, has become one of the best-known scenes in the Gospels, and its textual history is set out below.
historical:
The account of the woman caught in adultery (7:53-8:11) has a history unlike any other passage in the Gospels. It is absent from every Greek manuscript of John earlier than about AD 400: from the two oldest papyri of John, Papyrus 66 (about AD 200) and Papyrus 75 (early third century), both in the Bodmer collection; from Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, the great parchment Bibles of the fourth century; and from the fifth-century codices W and T. Codex Alexandrinus and Codex Ephraemi are damaged at this point, but calculations of the space on their missing leaves show that they could not have contained it. Codices L and Δ (eighth and ninth centuries) omit it but leave a blank space, as though the scribe knew of it. It is also missing from the oldest Syriac versions, the Sinaitic and Curetonian manuscripts and the best copies of the Peshitta, from the Coptic versions, and from several Old Latin manuscripts, while other Old Latin copies include it. The first surviving Greek manuscript to contain it is Codex Bezae, a Greek and Latin manuscript copied around AD 400. After that it spreads, and it is found in most later Byzantine manuscripts; more than 1,400 Greek manuscripts now contain it.

Where it appears, it does not always stand in the same place. Most manuscripts put it after 7:52, but manuscript 225 places it after 7:36, several Georgian manuscripts after 7:44, the group of manuscripts called family 1 at the end of John after 21:25, and the group called family 13 in Luke, after Luke 21:38, where Jesus spends his nights on the Mount of Olives and the people come to him early in the temple. Many manuscripts that contain it mark it with asterisks or obeli, the signs ancient scribes used for doubtful text. Its vocabulary is unlike John's: scribes (grammateis) appear nowhere else in John, nor does the Mount of Olives, and several words and phrases are closer to Luke's style. In the Byzantine church's reading calendar the Pentecost lesson ran from 7:37 to 7:52 and then skipped to 8:12, and 8:3-11 was read instead on the feast of penitent women such as Saint Pelagia on October 8, which may help explain how a separate story came to rest here.

The story was nevertheless known early. Eusebius reports that Papias, bishop of Hierapolis in the early second century, told a story about a woman accused of many sins before the Lord, which Eusebius says was also contained in the Gospel according to the Hebrews (Ecclesiastical History 3.39.17). A Syrian church order of the third century, the Didascalia Apostolorum, tells bishops to follow the example of the Lord, who sent away a woman who had sinned without condemning her. Didymus the Blind, teaching in Alexandria in the fourth century, knew a version of it found, he says, in certain gospels (Commentary on Ecclesiastes 223, from the papyri found at Tura in 1941). Ambrose preached it in Milan. Jerome included it in his Latin revision of the Gospels (about 383) and later wrote that it was found in many Greek and Latin copies of John (Against the Pelagians 2.17, about 415), and Augustine suggested that some men of little faith had removed it from their copies, fearing it would give their wives license to sin (On Adulterous Marriages 2.6-7, about 419). The first Greek commentator to discuss it is Euthymius Zigabenus in the twelfth century, who notes that the accurate copies either lack it or mark it with an obelus.

The main discourse (8:12-59) is set in the temple, “near the treasury” (8:20). The Mishnah describes thirteen offering chests shaped like trumpets for the temple's collections (m. Shekalim 6:5), and Mark places them where the widow gave her two coins (Mark 12:41-44), which most scholars locate in the Court of the Women. That was also where, during Tabernacles, the great lamps were lit (m. Sukkah 5:2-3). Whether the Jewish authorities could carry out a stoning in Roman Judea is debated. John says they could not lawfully execute anyone (18:31), and the Jerusalem Talmud preserves a tradition that the right to try capital cases was taken from Israel forty years before the temple's destruction (y. Sanhedrin 1:1). But Rome allowed the death penalty for Gentiles who entered the inner courts, as the Greek warning inscriptions from the temple show, one of which was found in 1871, and the stoning of Stephen (Acts 7:58) and of Jesus' brother James in AD 62 (Josephus, Antiquities 20.200) show that mob or irregular executions still happened. The attempted stoning in 8:59 is of that kind.
cultural:
The law of Moses prescribed death for adultery, for both the man and the woman (Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 22:22). Stoning is specified for the case of a betrothed woman (Deuteronomy 22:23-24) and is the punishment Ezekiel pictures for an unfaithful wife (Ezekiel 16:38-40); the Mishnah later assigns strangling for adultery with a married woman (m. Sanhedrin 11:1) and stoning for a betrothed girl (m. Sanhedrin 7:4), so the accusers' claim that Moses commanded stoning (8:5) may point to a betrothed woman or may reflect the older practice. Conviction required two or three witnesses to the act itself (Deuteronomy 17:6, 19:15), and by the time of the Mishnah the rules of evidence had made capital sentences extremely rare. The accusers bring only the woman, though the law condemned both, which shows the charge was more about trapping Jesus than about justice. The trap had two jaws. If Jesus said to stone her, he would appear harsh and would defy Roman rule; if he said to release her, he could be accused of setting aside Moses. What Jesus wrote on the ground isn't recorded. Jerome thought he wrote the accusers' sins, recalling Jeremiah 17:13, where those who turn away from the Lord are written in the dust; others have suggested the words of Exodus 23:1 or simply a deliberate refusal to answer on their terms. The text does not say.

In the discourse, the Pharisees object that testimony about oneself is not valid (8:13). The law required two witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15), and the Mishnah states the principle that a person is not believed when testifying about himself (m. Ketubbot 2:9). Jesus answers on their terms: he and the Father are two witnesses (8:17-18). The debate about Abraham turns on descent. To be a child of Abraham was the heart of Israel's identity and hope, since God's promises were made to him and his offspring (Genesis 12:1-3, 15:5, 17:7), and John the Baptist had already warned that descent from Abraham was no protection (Matthew 3:9). The hearers' claim never to have been slaves (8:33) is striking in a people who remembered Egypt at every Passover and lived under Rome; Josephus has Eleazar, the leader at Masada, say that they had long ago resolved to serve neither the Romans nor anyone else but God (Jewish War 7.323), and the claim here is probably meant in that spirit, as a statement of inner freedom under God. Jesus argues that true sonship is shown by resembling the father in deeds, a common ancient idea: a son does what his father does (5:19).

The insults are pointed. The retort “We are not illegitimate children” (8:41) may be a jab at rumors about Jesus' own birth; the second-century critic Celsus, as quoted by Origen, repeated a Jewish story that Jesus was born of adultery (Against Celsus 1.28, 1.32), though whether John's readers would hear that here is debated. To call Jesus a Samaritan (8:48) was to call him a heretic and an outsider, since Samaritans rejected the Jerusalem temple (4:9, 4:20), and to say he had a demon was to call him mad or possessed (7:20, 10:20). The remark that he is “not yet fifty years old” (8:57) is a round number for a man not yet old; fifty was the age at which Levites retired from service (Numbers 4:3). Stones for throwing (8:59) were close to hand in a temple still under construction, and stoning was the law's penalty for blasphemy (Leviticus 24:16).
literary:
The main discourse (8:12-59) is a running debate, the sharpest in the Gospel, built on a chain of challenges and replies. It falls into three rounds. In the first (8:12-20) the issue is testimony; in the second (8:21-30) it is origin, from above or from below, and the need to believe; in the third (8:31-59) it is freedom, fatherhood, and Abraham. Each round ends with a narrative note: no one seized him because his hour had not come (8:20), many believed in him (8:30), and they picked up stones (8:59). The dialogue escalates as the hearers move from questions to insults to violence, and Jesus' claims escalate in step.

The chapter turns on the phrase “I am” (Greek egō eimi). It first appears with a predicate, “I am the light of the world” (8:12), the second of John's seven sayings with an image. Then it stands alone: “unless you believe that I am He” (8:24), “then you will know that I am He” (8:28), where the BSB supplies He, and finally “before Abraham was born, I am” (8:58). These absolute uses echo God's words in the Greek Old Testament, where God says ‘I am’ of himself (Deuteronomy 32:39) and tells Israel to know and believe that ‘I am’ (Isaiah 43:10), and they recall God's self-naming to Moses (Exodus 3:14). The contrast in 8:58 is sharpened by the verbs: Abraham came to be (genesthai), but Jesus simply is. Psalm 90:2 speaks the same way of God: before the mountains came to be, you are. The stones in 8:59 show the hearers understood the claim.

Misunderstanding drives the dialogue, as elsewhere in John. When Jesus says he is going where they cannot come, they wonder whether he will kill himself (8:22); when he speaks of freedom, they hear politics and ancestry (8:33); when he promises that his word gives victory over death, they hear madness (8:52). The themes of witness, judging, freedom and slavery, fatherhood, truth and lies weave together throughout, and the word truth (alētheia) occurs seven times. The adultery story is a different kind of writing: a compact scene of conflict with a trap, a silence, a single saying, and a dismissal, very like the controversy stories of the Synoptic Gospels (compare Mark 12:13-17).

outline.t: The woman caught in adultery (absent from the earliest manuscripts)
I am the light of the world; the Father testifies
From above: unless you believe that I am He
The truth will set you free
Children of Abraham, children of God, or of the devil
Before Abraham was born, I am

doctrines.note: The absolute “I am” sayings (8:24, 28, 58) take up the name God revealed to Moses (Exodus 3:14) and his self-declarations in Isaiah (43:10, 25). John presents this as the core of Christian confession: Jesus is not a created being who began to exist, but the one who is before Abraham.

“Everyone who sins is a slave to sin” (8:34). Sin here is not only a wrong act but a bondage that no descent or religious standing can break, and those who reject the Son will die in their sins (8:21, 24). The hearers insist they have never been slaves, and the chapter shows how sin blinds people to their own condition.

Freedom comes from the Son: “if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed” (8:36). It is received by continuing in his word (8:31), which marks true disciples, and it brings victory over death (8:51). In the adultery account, mercy comes first and the call to holiness follows it: “Then neither do I condemn you” and “Now go and sin no more.”

Jesus says he judges no one according to the flesh, yet his judgment is true because the Father is with him (8:15-16), and he has much to judge (8:26). The Father is the one who seeks his glory and judges (8:50). In the adultery account the would-be judges are themselves judged by a single sentence, and the only one without sin declines to condemn.

The debate over who are Abraham's true children (8:33-47) asks what makes someone a member of God's people. Jesus grants their descent (8:37) but says Abraham's children do Abraham's works and rejoice in his day (8:39, 56). Paul makes a related argument about Abraham's offspring in Romans 4 and 9 and Galatians 3.

words.note: Eimi, to be. It is one of the commonest Greek verbs, used some 2,400 times in the New Testament, but in John the first person egō eimi (I am) carries special weight. It appears with images (bread, light, door, shepherd, resurrection, way, vine) and, in this chapter, without any predicate (8:24, 28, 58). In 8:58 the contrast is sharp: before Abraham came to be (the aorist infinitive of ginomai), Jesus says not ‘I was’ but ‘I am’, a present that speaks of existence without beginning.

Phōs, light. It occurs about 73 times in the New Testament and 23 times in John. In the Bible light stands for God's presence, truth, and salvation (Psalm 27:1; Isaiah 9:2; 49:6), and Israel in the wilderness followed a pillar of fire by night (Exodus 13:21), which the lamps of Tabernacles recalled. John's prologue calls the Word the true light coming into the world (1:9). Here Jesus claims it of himself, and chapter 9 shows it in action as he gives sight to a man born blind.

Martyria, testimony or witness. It occurs about 37 times in the New Testament and 14 times in John, more than in any other Gospel, together with the verb martyreō (to testify). John's Gospel is built like a trial, with witnesses called for Jesus: John the Baptist, his works, the Scriptures, the Father, and later the Spirit and the disciples (5:31-39, 15:26-27). In 8:13-18 the Pharisees dispute his testimony, and Jesus answers that his own witness joins the Father's.

Hamartia, sin, originally a missing of the mark. It occurs about 173 times in the New Testament and 17 times in John. In John sin is above all the refusal to believe in the Son (16:9), and it is a condition as well as an act: in 8:21 Jesus speaks of dying in ‘your sin’ (singular), in 8:24 of ‘your sins’ (plural). The word ties the adultery story, with its challenge to anyone ‘without sin’ (anamartētos), to the discourse on slavery to sin (8:34) and to Jesus' question, ‘Which of you can prove Me guilty of sin?’ (8:46).

Alētheia, truth. It occurs about 109 times in the New Testament and 25 times in John, seven of them in this chapter. BDAG notes both the sense of what is true as opposed to false and the sense of reality, and John uses both. Truth is the reality of God made known, and Jesus will say that he himself is the truth (14:6). The truth that sets free (8:32) is not an idea but a relationship with the one who speaks it; the devil, by contrast, does not stand in the truth (8:44).

Eleutheroō, to set free. It occurs seven times in the New Testament, twice here (8:32, 36) and five times in Paul (Romans 6:18, 22; 8:2, 21; Galatians 5:1). The hearers take it politically and ethnically, as if Jesus called them slaves of a foreign master, but Jesus means freedom from sin. The word recalls the exodus, when God freed Israel from slavery, and Paul uses it in the same sense of freedom from sin and death.

Doulos, slave or servant. It occurs about 124 times in the New Testament. In the ancient household a slave belonged to the house but had no permanent place in it and could be sold, while a son belonged to it forever (8:35). Jesus uses that picture: those enslaved to sin have no secure place in God's household, but the Son can give them a son's freedom. Compare Galatians 4:1-7, where Paul uses the same contrast between slave and son.

Katakrinō, to condemn or pass sentence against. It occurs about 18 times in the New Testament, in John only in 8:10-11. Jesus asks the woman whether anyone has condemned her, and then says, “Then neither do I condemn you”. The refusal is not a denial of her sin, since he adds, “Now go and sin no more”; it is a refusal to pass the sentence that the accusers wanted and that the law allowed. It echoes 3:17: the Son was not sent to condemn the world but to save it.

christ:
This chapter contains some of the plainest claims to deity in the Gospels. Jesus is the light of the world that Isaiah promised would reach the nations (Isaiah 42:6, 49:6), spoken at the feast whose lamps lit all Jerusalem and recalled the pillar of fire that led Israel through the wilderness. Whoever follows him, as Israel followed the pillar, will not walk in darkness (8:12). He is from above and not of this world (8:23). His testimony is joined to the Father's, and he always does what pleases the Father (8:29), so that knowing him is knowing the Father (8:19). He will be lifted up (8:28), John's double word for crucifixion and exaltation (3:14, 12:32-33), and in that lifting people will know that I am. The cross, in John, is where the divine identity of Jesus is most clearly shown.

He is the Son who alone can make slaves free (8:36), the one without sin (8:46), whose word conquers death (8:51). He claims that Abraham, the father of Israel, rejoiced to see his day (8:56). Jewish tradition remembered Abraham as a man to whom God revealed the future: 4 Ezra 3:14 says God showed him the end of the times secretly by night, and the Book of Jubilees has Abraham rejoicing greatly at the birth of Isaac and keeping the first Feast of Tabernacles with joy (Jubilees 16:19-31). Jesus says the day Abraham saw and rejoiced in was his. And then, “before Abraham was born, I am” (8:58): he speaks the name of God as his own. The church confesses what the hearers rejected: that the man standing in the temple is the eternal Son, of one being with the Father.

Whatever the textual history of the adultery account, the church has remembered in it a true picture of Jesus. He refuses to condemn a sinner whom others wanted to use as a trap and kill, while calling her to a new life, which is exactly what the rest of the Gospel says he came to do (3:17). The one without sin is the only one entitled to throw the stone, and he does not. At the cross he will bear the judgment himself.
interpretation:
The woman caught in adultery has been read in the Latin West since Ambrose and Augustine. Augustine preached on it in his Tractates on John (33, around 414), where he says that when the accusers had gone, two were left, misery and mercy; Pope Francis took that phrase as the title of his apostolic letter Misericordia et misera (2016), which closed the Jubilee Year of Mercy. Jerome, as noted, thought Jesus wrote the accusers' sins in the dust, recalling Jeremiah 17:13, and a few late manuscripts add at 8:8 that he wrote the sins of each of them. In the East the passage entered the liturgy on the feast of penitent women. The Council of Trent (1546) received the books of Scripture with all their parts as they were read in the church and contained in the Latin Vulgate, and Roman Catholic teaching has since treated the passage as canonical. Calvin, in his commentary on John (1553), noted that the passage was unknown to the ancient Greek churches but expounded it as a true account. Among modern studies, Bart Ehrman (New Testament Studies, 1988) argued that two earlier stories, one known to Papias and the Didascalia and one known to Didymus, merged into the form now in John; Chris Keith (The Pericope Adulterae, the Gospel of John, and the Literacy of Jesus, 2009) argued it was inserted in the third century partly to show Jesus as able to write; and Jennifer Knust and Tommy Wasserman (To Cast the First Stone, 2018) traced its whole history of transmission and use.

In art the scene has been painted many times. Pieter Bruegel the Elder's small grisaille of 1565, now in the Courtauld Gallery in London, shows Jesus writing on the ground in Dutch the words of 8:7, and Rembrandt's Woman Taken in Adultery (1644), in the National Gallery in London, sets the scene in the vast shadowed temple with Christ and the woman in the light. Lucas Cranach, Titian, Tintoretto, and Poussin painted it too.

The discourse of 8:12-59 was central to the church's debates about Christ. Athanasius and other fourth-century defenders of the Council of Nicaea (325) cited 8:58 against the Arians, who taught that the Son had a beginning, and Augustine (Tractates on John 34-43) read the ‘I am’ as the divine name. The verse ‘the truth will set you free’ (8:32) is one of the most quoted lines of the Bible in public life; it is the motto of Johns Hopkins University and is carved in the lobby of the original headquarters of the Central Intelligence Agency, usually with its first condition, continuing in Jesus' word, forgotten. Lutheran churches read 8:31-36 on Reformation Day.

The chapter's darkest legacy is 8:44. Martin Luther cited it in On the Jews and Their Lies (1543), and it was repeated in medieval and modern anti-Jewish polemic and in Nazi propaganda, including children's literature. After the Holocaust, scholars such as Rosemary Radford Ruether (Faith and Fratricide, 1974) and Adele Reinhartz have pressed the church to reckon with how the verse has been used, and the Second Vatican Council's declaration Nostra Aetate (1965) taught that Jews must not be presented as rejected or accursed by God. Luke Timothy Johnson (Journal of Biblical Literature, 1989) set such language within the conventions of ancient polemic between rival groups.
text:
The largest textual question in this chapter is 7:53-8:11, the story of the woman caught in adultery, whose manuscript history is set out in the historical note. In brief, it is absent from all the earliest Greek manuscripts and versions, first appears in a Greek manuscript around AD 400 (Codex Bezae), wanders among several locations in John and Luke in the manuscripts that have it, and is often marked with signs of doubt. The King James Version (1611), following the late Greek manuscripts of its day, prints it without any mark. The first edition of the Revised Standard Version New Testament (1946) removed it from the running text; the second edition (1971) restored it, set apart with a note. Today the ESV and NRSV print it within double brackets, the NASB within brackets, and the NIV sets it off with a note that the earliest manuscripts and many other ancient witnesses do not have it. The BSB prints it with a note, and this Bible marks the verses as a later addition. Among editions of the Greek text, the Nestle-Aland text prints it within double brackets, the SBL Greek New Testament (2010) leaves it out of its main text, and the Byzantine and Textus Receptus editions include it without marks. A handful of scholars, notably Maurice Robinson, defend it as part of John's original Gospel. Within the passage the manuscripts that contain it differ from one another more than is usual; in 8:6, for example, some have a compound verb sometimes used of writing down a record, and others the simple verb to write.

In the discourse, verse 25 is a famous puzzle. The Greek is ambiguous, and it has been rendered ‘Just what I have been telling you from the beginning’ (BSB, similar to the ESV and NIV), ‘Why do I speak to you at all?’ (an old reading noted in the New American Bible and elsewhere), or ‘I am what I have told you from the start’. Papyrus 66, in a correction, reads ‘I told you at the beginning what I am also telling you now’. In verse 57 Papyrus 75 and the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus read ‘and has Abraham seen you?’, which makes the retort answer 8:56 directly; most manuscripts read ‘have you seen Abraham?’ At the end of verse 59 the King James Version adds ‘going through the midst of them, and so passed by’, words from later manuscripts that echo Luke 4:30. In 8:58 nearly all English versions render the present tense ‘I am’, but a few, among them James Moffatt's translation (1913) and the New World Translation of the Jehovah's Witnesses, render it ‘I have existed’ or ‘I have been’, which obscures the contrast with Abraham's coming to be and the echo of the divine name.

teach.big: Jesus, the eternal I Am, is the light of the world who alone can free people from slavery to sin, and he meets sinners not with the condemnation they deserve but with mercy that calls them to a new life.

outline.t: Religious zeal can use a person as a pawn, and a trap set for Jesus exposes the accusers more than the accused.
Jesus' one sentence turns every accuser to self-examination, and the oldest are the first to see it.
The only one without sin refuses to condemn, and his mercy comes with a call to leave sin behind.
Jesus is the light of the world, and his testimony is true because the Father stands with him.
Those who reject the one from above die in their sins; in his lifting up he will be known as I Am.
True discipleship is continuing in Jesus' word, and only the Son can free slaves of sin.
Real kinship with Abraham and with God is shown by love for the one God sent, and rejection of truth reveals whose likeness we bear.
Abraham rejoiced to see Jesus' day, because Jesus is the eternal I Am who existed before Abraham came to be.

teach.pitfalls:
With the adultery story, teachers should be honest about its textual history, neither hiding it nor using it to cast doubt on the rest of the Gospels. The passage is not evidence that Jesus set aside the moral law or regarded adultery lightly; he tells the woman to sin no more. Nor does 8:7 forbid all judgment, church discipline, or courts of law; it confronts hypocrisy and the abuse of the law to destroy a person. Speculation about what Jesus wrote, however interesting, should not become the sermon.

With 8:12-59, the great danger is reading 8:44 as a statement about Jewish people. The hearers are identified as those who had believed in him (8:31) and who now seek to kill him (8:37, 40); the verse describes their action, not their ancestry, and Jesus speaks the same kind of language to Peter (Mark 8:33) and about Judas (6:70). Teachers should name the verse's shameful history plainly. Avoid, too, detaching 8:32 from 8:31: the truth that sets free is known by those who continue in Jesus' word, not a general promise that knowledge liberates.
teach.pastoral: The adultery story will press on anyone who has been publicly shamed, sexually exposed, or treated as an object by people with power, and on those whose sexual sin is known. Notice that the man is absent and the woman is made to stand in front of a crowd; teach it with care for those who have been blamed while others escaped. It will also reach people who cannot stop condemning themselves: Jesus' words ‘neither do I condemn you’ come before ‘go and sin no more’, not after, and the scrupulous need to hear that order. Jewish listeners, and Christians who love Jewish friends, will be listening closely to how 8:44 is handled.

hard.q: Should the story of the woman caught in adultery be in the Bible?
hard.a:
The case against treating it as part of John is strong, and its defenders include most textual critics across traditions. Bruce Metzger, in his Textual Commentary on the Greek New Testament (1971), called it a floating piece of tradition that circulated in parts of the Western church and was later inserted into manuscripts at various places. It is absent from all the earliest manuscripts and versions, the earliest Greek commentators on John pass over it, it moves among several locations in the manuscripts that include it, and its style is unlike John's. Bart Ehrman (Misquoting Jesus, 2005) presents it as a leading example of how scribes changed the text, and Daniel Wallace, an evangelical textual critic, has argued (New Testament Studies, 1993, replying to John Paul Heil's case for its Johannine style) that its language and placement show it was not part of John's Gospel. Skeptical readers add that if a passage this famous was added later, readers should ask what else was.

Others respond in several ways. A small group of scholars, including Maurice Robinson and earlier Zane Hodges, defend it as part of John's Gospel from the start, arguing that it was removed in some regions, as Augustine suggested, because it seemed to excuse adultery. Many more, including most evangelical, Catholic, and critical scholars, accept that it was not part of John as first written but hold that it preserves an early and likely genuine memory of Jesus. It was known in the second century to Papias and in the third to the Didascalia, it fits what the Gospels elsewhere show of Jesus' dealings with sinners and his opponents' traps (compare Mark 12:13-17), and its apparent leniency troubled some early readers, which makes it an unlikely invention. Chris Keith and Knust and Wasserman have shown how long and how widely the church read and valued it.

Churches handle it differently. Roman Catholic teaching regards it as canonical Scripture; the Eastern churches read it in their liturgy; many Protestant scholars treat it as a true account about Jesus that can be taught with a clear note about its history, while others think it should not be preached as Scripture in the full sense. Nothing in Christian doctrine depends on this passage alone, and its teaching of mercy joined to a call to holiness is found throughout the Gospels. As for the skeptic's question, the case of this passage shows that textual critics can detect such additions, because the manuscript evidence is abundant and early; the only other passage of comparable length whose place is in similar doubt is the longer ending of Mark (16:9-20). The course most Bibles now follow is to print it, mark it, and explain it.

hard.q: When Jesus says, “You belong to your father, the devil” (8:44), is the Gospel of John anti-Jewish?
hard.a:
The objection deserves to be stated at full strength. John's Gospel uses the word Ioudaioi, the Jews, about seventy times, often for those who oppose Jesus, and here Jesus tells them that their father is the devil, a murderer and liar. Rosemary Radford Ruether (Faith and Fratricide, 1974) argued that anti-Judaism is built into Christian claims about Christ, and Adele Reinhartz, a Jewish scholar of John, has argued (Cast Out of the Covenant, 2018) that John's rhetoric invites readers to separate themselves from the Jews and to see them as outside God's covenant. The verse's history supports the charge that it has been read that way. It fed centuries of Christian contempt for Jews, was cited by Martin Luther in On the Jews and Their Lies (1543), and was used in Nazi propaganda. Jewish readers do not need to be persuaded that this verse has been dangerous.

Christian scholars respond in several ways, while granting that history. First, the context is specific: Jesus is speaking to “the Jews who had believed Him” (8:31) who now seek to kill him (8:37, 40), and the charge concerns what they are doing, not their birth. Jesus himself, his disciples, and the Gospel's author are Jews, and the same Gospel says that salvation is from the Jews (4:22). Second, the language belongs to fierce disputes within Judaism. The Dead Sea Scrolls tell the community to hate the sons of darkness and curse the men of the lot of Belial, meaning other Jews outside the community (1QS 1:9-10, 2:4-5), Israel's own prophets used harsh words against their people (Isaiah 1:4, 57:3), and Luke Timothy Johnson (Journal of Biblical Literature, 1989) showed that such slander was conventional in ancient polemic between rival schools. Third, the New Testament applies the same language to insiders: Jesus calls Peter Satan (Mark 8:33) and Judas a devil (6:70), and 1 John 3:8-10 says anyone who does not do right is a child of the devil. Raymond Brown and many others have argued that John's hostility reflects the painful separation between the church and the synagogue late in the first century (compare 9:22).

These responses explain the verse without erasing the damage done with it. The Second Vatican Council's Nostra Aetate (1965) and many Protestant bodies have taught that the Jewish people are not to be presented as rejected or accursed, and the verse gives no Christian warrant for contempt. The church reads it rightly when it hears in it a warning to every reader, Christian first of all, about what happens when religious people reject the truth and seek to destroy the one who speaks it.

observe: Whom do the scribes and Pharisees bring to Jesus, whom do they leave out, and in what order do the accusers leave?
What does Jesus say about his testimony and the Father's testimony in 8:13-18?
What do the hearers claim about Abraham and about their freedom, and how does Jesus answer each claim?
interpret: Why do you think Jesus says ‘neither do I condemn you’ before ‘go and sin no more’, rather than the other way around?
What does Jesus mean when he says the truth will set you free, and why do his hearers insist they have never been slaves?
Why did the crowd pick up stones when Jesus said, ‘before Abraham was born, I am’? What did they understand him to be claiming?
apply: The accusers leave one by one, oldest first. What would it take for you to recognize yourself in Jesus' words about the one without sin?
Where might you be bound in ways you are reluctant to admit, and what would continuing in Jesus' word look like there?
Jesus' strongest words are aimed at people who had believed in him. What is the difference in your own life between initial belief and continuing in his word?
